problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r=\sqrt{1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2}$ ?

activity_context.topic_title: Further Properties of Line Integrals of Scalar Functions

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14093452/assets/d33f9b851125443ff738fa4c3aedcbeaf8a202d05caa06747e74262c0ae89bd9.png)

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={e}^{2\theta }\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{2},$ shown above.
feedback.worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={e}^{2\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=2{e}^{2\theta }.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{({e}^{2\theta })}^{2}+{(2{e}^{2\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{{e}^{4\theta }+4{e}^{4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\sqrt{5{e}^{4\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{e}^{2\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}{e}^{2\theta }{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}({e}^{\pi }-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}({e}^{\pi }-1)\end{aligned}
$$
